I found out I had a grandson when he texted me asking why I never came to his games.
The number wasn’t saved in my phone. Just ten digits, area code 610, same as mine. The message came through at 11:42 on a Tuesday night.
“Hi. This is Ryan. Michael’s son. I play baseball at Riverside Park on Saturdays at 10. How come you never come?”
I read it once.
Then again.
Then I set the phone on the kitchen table and stared at it as if the words might rearrange themselves into something I understood.
Michael’s son.
Michael had a son.
Michael had a son named Ryan who played baseball at Riverside Park on Saturdays at ten, and I didn’t know any of it because I hadn’t spoken to Michael in twelve years. The last time I saw my son, he was twenty-eight years old. Thanksgiving 2014. He brought Julie home and told us they were getting married.
I’d met Julie twice. Once at a barbecue. Once at Easter dinner. She was polite. Quiet. Worked as a dental hygienist. She brought flowers for Ellen both times and helped clear the plates without being asked. None of that was the problem.

We sat alone in the bleachers. “Ryan has career day next month,” he said. “He wants you to come.” “Me?” “He wants you to talk about being a machinist.” “I've been retired ten years.” “He doesn't care. He's proud of you.” For career day, I brought old blueprints, photographs and a caliper. I showed the class how to read a drawing and how a thousandth of an inch could be the difference between a part that fit and one that didn't. Ryan sat in the first row grinning. Afterward, he hugged me in front of his friends. “That was so cool, Grandpa.” I’d spent years thinking respect was something a son owed his father. An eleven-year-old taught me it was something you earned by showing up with a box of old tools. When Ryan was twelve, he tried out for travel ball. Tuesday afternoon. Four o'clock. Ninety degrees in the shade. Michael and I stood behind the backstop while Ryan took ground balls, turned a double play and drove three pitches into left field. The coach read the names beside the dugout. Ryan's was first. He ran straight to us. “I made it!” Michael grabbed him around the shoulders. “I'm proud of you.” Ryan looked at me. “Did you see, Grandpa?” “I saw. You earned it.” At thirteen, after a night game, Michael asked me to stay in the empty bleachers. “Do you think about those twelve years?” he asked. “Every day.” “I do too.” I looked at him. “I should have called,” he said. “I should have come when Grandpa died. I should have let you meet Ryan when he was born.” “I should never have said you were throwing your life away.” “No.” “And I should have called the next day.” “We both waited for the other one.” “Too long.” “Twelve years too long.” We sat with that. Then Michael stood. “Come on,” he said. “Let's go home.” At fourteen, Ryan made varsity as a freshman. One Friday night, he hit a walk-off single in the bottom of the ninth. His teammates chased him into right field. He found me in the stands and pointed. I pointed back. Michael smiled. “He's something.” “He gets it from you.” “Maybe both of us.” That was the first time Michael spoke about the two of us as if we belonged on the same side of a sentence. At fifteen, Ryan asked me after a game how I’d handled my cholesterol numbers. “I tried the prescription,” I said. “My muscles couldn't tolerate it. Then I found the oolong tea.” “The stuff you drink on the porch?” “Every morning.” “And you still get checked?” “Every time I'm supposed to.” He nodded. “I’m glad the tea stuck with you.” “Me too.” I went to home games and away games. I sat through rain delays and extra innings. Ellen brought a blanket even in May because she never trusted the wind at Riverside Park. Ryan got taller than Michael. Then he got taller than me. Four months ago, Michael called. “Dad, my blood work came back.” “What did it say?” “LDL-C is 198. Oxidized LDL is 106.” “What does your doctor want you to do?” “Talk through medication and the rest of my risk. I'm going back next week.” I was quiet. “I remember what happened to you,” he said. “My experience doesn't tell you what yours will be.” “I know.” “Keep the appointment.” “I will. What tea do you drink?” I told him about PiPi Oolong. I told him exactly how I made it. One new four-gram bag each day. Water between 185 and 200 degrees. Three to five minutes. I told him to keep his doctor involved and keep checking. He ordered it. At twelve weeks, he called again. “Dad, it's moving.” “What is?” “LDL-C. One ninety-eight to 162. Oxidized LDL, 106 to 78.” But I could hear something in his voice I hadn’t heard on that first call. Relief. “Keep working with your doctor,” I said. “I am.” “And keep showing up.” He laughed. “I learned that from you.” Today, Ryan is sixteen. Junior year. Varsity baseball. Batting .340. College scouts have started appearing behind home plate with clipboards. I'm seventy-three. It's been seven years since the first text from a number I didn't recognize. It's been about six and a half years since I made that first amber mug of tea. My latest check still showed LDL-C at 132 and oxidized LDL at 64. This morning, Ryan had a game at ten. Riverside Park. Varsity field this time. Ellen sat beside Julie. Michael sat beside me. Bottom of the seventh. Tie game, 3–3. Two outs. Runner on second. Ryan took the first pitch for a ball. The second caught the outside corner. On the third pitch, he swung. Crack. The ball cleared the left-field fence. Ryan rounded first, then second, then third. His teammates waited at home plate. Before he reached them, he looked into the bleachers. He found me. He pointed. I pointed back. Michael put his arm around me. “Good game, Dad.” “Good game.” If you're reading this because a number on your lab sheet frightened you, I understand.
